The resulting TOU rate has lower prices both overnight (midnight to 7 a.m. on weekdays and midnight to 9 a.m. on weekend days) and on weekends. Because we only use one TOU rate in this study, in what follows, we refer to the TOU-1-2 rate as “TOU.”3 Because individual vehicles (or drivers or chargers) achieve RTP- and TOU-based EVMC by scheduling charging to communicated prices, RTP and TOU can access individual vehicles’ full flexibility. Price-responsive mechanisms’ ability to access each individual vehicle’s full flexibility is an advantage compared to scaled forms of aggregate DLC. However, many vehicles receiving the same prices are incentivized to act synchronously. This can result in large load spikes as vehicles respond to RTP minimums, or large jumps or drops in EV charging at the times when TOU rates change. This study mitigates TOU charging spikes by flattening EV price-response with a $1/(MW/h) ramp penalty. The ramp penalty creates a preference, for example, for an EV needing p kWh to charge at p/4 kW in 4 equally priced hours (for a total ramp penalty of $0.0005p) rather than p in the first hour and 0 in the following 3 hours (for a total ramp penalty of $0.002p). Although not widely implemented today, such a management strategy could be implemented by local controllers aware of vehicles’ planned departure times and desired SOCs, in addition to the TOU rate schedule. Our results show that this flattening of EVMC response to TOU rates is a primary way price-responsive mechanisms can work at higher shares of LDVs participating in EVMC. 2.5 Production Cost Modeling Implementation This study uses production cost modeling in up to three nested scheduling stages in the PLEXOS software to simulate the impact of different EVMC participation, flexibility, and dispatch mechanism scenarios on bulk power system operating costs. Stages 1 and 2 mimic two- settlement wholesale electricity market formulations common in North America, including in ISO-NE. Stage 1 is a day-ahead unit commitment and economic dispatch simulation that fixes most unit commitments for Stage 2 based on nodal transmission constraints and fixed load forecasts. Stage 2 is a real-time simulation that accepts Stage 1 commitment and dispatch decisions as input and then responds to actual load conditions by changing the commitment status of fast-starting combustion turbines and adjusting committed generators’ dispatch levels. All scenarios use Stage 1 and Stage 2 simulations, with different Stage 1 results feeding into Stage 2 based on the EVMC dispatch mechanism and forecast type. Only low-error DLC (DLC- LE) scenarios start with Stage 0, which performs regional, day-ahead unit commitment and economic dispatch including the aggregate, megawatt-scale DLC-LE flexibility resources described in Section 2.3.
